November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Minnie D. Middleton, of the District of Columbia, who served as a clerk in the War Department for a period of 12 years, may be reinstated in the classified service and appointed to a clerkship at $900 in the Department of State, notwithstand- ing the lapse of more than one year since her separation from the service. Mrs. Middleton’s service in the War Department was faithful and efficient. She is at present employed upon the temporary force of the State Department dealing with the relief of American citizens abroad, and this order is issued upon the recommenda- tion of the Secretary of State, who considers it in the interest of the public service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation. 
November 11, 1914. 
Horatio Whitted may he appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service without regard to the civil-service rules. Mr. Whitted was appointed as a la’ orer at $660 per annum on May 9, 1901, and assigned to the General Land Office, where he still is employed. It appears that, although his principal duties were of the grade performed by classified employees, his name was erroneously omitted from the list of such employees who were classified by the Executive orders of January 12, 1905, and March 30, 1905, and this order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Interior to correct the error. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation. 
November 16, 1914. 
William P. Fix may be appointed a skilled helper in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without compliance with the civil-service rules pertaining to that position, Mr. Fix was formerly a plate printer in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, but on account of a physical disability for the proper performance of the work of a printer was compelled to resign. A physical examination given by the Civil Service Commis- sion develops the fact that he is able to perform duty as a skilled helper. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury and is concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. 
November 17, 1914. 
Mrs. C. H. Brice may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is issued because of the fact that the main Suppor of Mrs. Brice and her young daughter was provided monthly 
by her brother, Col. Franklin J. Moses, United States Marine Corps, who lost his life in the line of duty on September 26,1914, in Vera Cruz. Mrs. Brice has passed a civil- service examination for clerk. : The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an Executive order in this case. 
November 21, 1914. 
The two sons of Hon. Julian Uribe Uribe, first vice president of the Colombian House of Representatives, may be employed on irrigation projects in the United States without regard to the provisions of the civil-service rules, for the purpose of learning through such employment the theory and practice of irrigation with a view ultimately to introducing this branch of science into the Colombian Republic. This order is issued in accordance with the principles of international comity and is recommended by the Acting Secretary of the Department of the Interior and by the Secretary of State. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Department of the Interior and the Department of State in recommending the issuance of the order. 
November 28, 1914. 
Miss Laura E. Scott may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service of the Department of State without examination under the civil-service rules. This action is based upon the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of State because of Miss Scott’s efficient service with several international arbitration com- missions, the exceptional qualifications she has evinced in the performance of her duties as confidential clerk to the Acting Secretary of State, and his representation that the loss of the services of Miss Scott, who has been with him in the capacity of confidential clerk for several years, would be a great inconvenience. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of this order.

December 1, 1914. 
Mrs. Orie Cummings may be appointed as a clerk in the Department of Agriculture without reference to the civil-service rules at a salary of $900 per annum. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Agriculture, who states that Mrs. Cummings’s training and experience are such as to enable her to render good service. She is the widow of Mr. R. F. Cummings, formerly a clerk at a salary of $1,400 per annum in the Bureau of Soils, Department of Agriculture. Mr. Cummings was in the service from October 16, 1906, until February 1, 1914, the date of his death. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation of the Secre- tary of Agriculture. 
December 7, 1914. 
Miss Louisa W. Happersett may be appointed to a position in the classified civil service without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that the Quartermaster General, the Surgeon General, and the Judge Advocate General of the Army unite in requesting the issuance of an Executive order. Miss Happersett is the daughter of the late John C. G. Happersett, major and surgeon, United States Army, who rendered highly efficient military service during a period of 32 years, including the 4 years of the Civil War. The Surgeon General and the Judge Advocate General call special attention to the services rendered by Maj. Happersett and his family during the yellow-fever epidemic at Fort Brown, Tex., in 1882. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the order.

Mrs. Sallie G. Jones, who has been employed in the Indian Bureau of the Interior Department for a period of four years, may be promoted without examination under the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, in view of the statement of the Judge Advocate General that he believes Mr. Lemmond to be especially qualified for the position of law clerk by reason of his education, training, and experience in legal work in the- Department of Justice. 
November 10, 1914. 
Mr. W. T. Bateman may be appointed a watchman in a navy yard without compli- ance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who says the case is a deserving one and that the general character of Mr. Bateman 1s such that he feels justified in recommending an exemption from the civil-service rules which 
will permit his employment in a navy yard so that he may be able to support his family. It appears that Mr. Bateman, seaman, formerly attached to the U. S. S. Foote, is at present a patient in the Naval Hospital, Washington, D. C. While visiting his family a l-pounder shell which he was showing his child exploded and blew off his left hand. The Surgeon General of the Navy concurs in the recommendation of the Sec- retary of the Navy and says Mr. Bateman is a very deserving man. While Mr. Bate- man will be discharged from the Navy for disability he can receive no pension, as his disability was not incurred in the line of duty. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of the order. 
November 10, 1914. : 
Mrs. Alice B. Smith and Mrs. Eunice B. Neff may be appointed to clerical positions in the classified service of the Post Office Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. Mrs. Smith is the, widow of John H. Smith, formerly a letter carrier at the Washing- ton post office, who served the Government continuously for 42 years and died as a result of three strokes of paralysis (possibly due to exposure while serving his route as a carrier) and left a widow and two small children without means of support. Mrs. Neff is the widow of W. E. Neff, a former employee of the Post Office Depart- ment, who, after 10 years’ faithful service, had a nervous breakdown, which resulted in insanity, and he recently died leaving three small children. Mrs. Neff is also the sole support of an aunt, who is an elderly woman. 
The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
November 10, 1914. 
Mr. Edwin B. Smith, who formerly held the position of clerk in the Interstate Com- merce Commission, may be reinstated to a classified position in the Post Office Depart- ment without regard to the length of his separation or the provisions of the civil-service rules requiring reinstatement in the same department. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Smith’s previous efficient service in the Interstate Commerce Commission and the exceptional qualifications he has evinced in the performance of his duties as confiden- tial clerk to the Postmaster General. 
November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Ellen McCabe Bain may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engrav- ing and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Bain served 11 years in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing; that she rendered efficient service there; and it is believed that her reinstatement will be in the interests of the service. The Civil Service Commission states that in view of Mrs. Bain’s 11 years of service, fairly recent separation, and the fact that she is not of advanced age, it will offer no 
objection to an Executive order being issued in her behalf. 
November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Annie Day may be appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service at the Government Printing Office without regard to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Day is the widow of Joseph P. Day, a former employee of the Government Printing Office, who in 1908 received an injury in line of duty which hastened his death and for which he received no compensation, as the law granting such payments for injuries received in the line of duty did not become effective until five weeks thereafter. EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 121 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who states that the position of Chief of the Division of Accounts is highly confidential, and requires a peculiar order of talent; that a diligent effort has been made within the classified service to find some one possessing the required qualifications, but without success. The Attorney General believes that Mr. Satterfield, who is known to him personally, is especially qualified for the position, and that the interests of the public would be subserved by exempting the appointment. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
January 5, 1915. 
Fred W. Carrington may be promoted from assistant messenger in the Pension Bureau to the clerical grade without examination under the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, in recognition of an ingenious and public-spirited employee who has built and put into operation a mechanical device and allowed the Government to take out patents for it. 
January 7, 1915. 
Mrs. Inez M. Clark and Miss Emily I. Kramer may be appointed clerks in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that on account of the technical character of the work required specially trained 
clerks are needed, and that Mrs. Clark and Miss Kramer have demonstrated that they possess the peculiar qualifications necessary. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
January 7, 1915. 
It is hereby ordered that the physical requirements be waived in order that Mr. George P. Kinsman, of the battleship Vermont, who lost his right leg as the result of injuries sustained during the occupation of Vera Cruz by the American troops in April, 1914, may take the clerk-carrier examination in the postal service. 
January 9, 1915. 
Mr. Charles A. Lyerly, jr., ishereby permitted to take the examination in accordance with law for appointment as second lieutenant in the Engineer Corps of the Army. He has passed the civil-service examination for junior engineer, but his eligibility has expired. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War and the Chief of Engineers, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
January 20, 1915. 
Mr. Newton C. Llewellyn may be reinstated as a carrier in the Knoxville, Tenn., post office without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Llewellyn entered the Postal Service as a substitute carrier at Knoxville on 
i 18, 1895, and remained in the service until February 28, 1907, when he resigned. 
The Postmaster General states that Mr. Llewellyn’s record is good, that it is a meritorious case, and that the department has no objection to the issuance of an order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. . 
January 21, 1915. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is extended to permit the rein- statement of Harold J. Wagner to a clerkship in the Department of Justice. Mr. Wagner was appointed through examination on June 26, 1905, as a clerk in the service of the Panama Canal, and served until June 9, 1906. On September 4, 1906, he was appointed to a clerkship in the Department of Justice, and served until April 9, 1909, when he resigned from the position of telegrapher and stenographer at $1,200 to accept a position on the Newfoundland Fisheries Arbitration Commission under the State Department. He continued in this position until September, 1910, when he was appointed secretary of the Chamizal Arbitration Commission under the State Department, in which position he served until the completion of the work in August, 1911. His duties in these positions are said to have been principally legal. He did not seek retransfer to the classified service because he was compelled to undergo an operation which incapacitated him for 15 months. From February 1 to June 30, 1914, he served as record clerk with the American-British Claims Arbitration Com- mission.

In view of the fact that Mr. Wagner was twice appointed through competitive examination, served for nearly four years in the classified service and for over two years in unclassified positions with a good record, the Civil Service Com- mission concurs in recommending the issuance of an order which involves merely the waiving of the year limit upon eligibility. uties 
January 21, 1915. 
Mr. James Hands, an unclassified laborer at $660 per annum in the office of the super- intendent of the State, War, and Navy Department Building, may be promoted to the position of classified laborer at $840 per annum in said office, without reference to civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that he is informed by the superintendent that on account of the special experi- ence in electrical work gained by Mr. Hands since his employment in August, 1906, he is better qualified to perform the duties of the position of skilled laborer than an eligible who would be secured from the skilled-laborer register of the Civil Service Commission; that he has made a study of electrical work, and in addition is familiar with the building and operation of the electrical force. The superintendent speaks in the highest terms of Mr. Hands’s record as a workman, and considers him well qualified to perform the duties of a skilled laborer assigned with the electrician as helper. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of this order. 
February 4, 1915. 
Mr. Ralph Izard, who was dismissed from the position of Chinese inspector in the Immigration Service February 3, 1903, may be reinstated to the position of immigrant inspector in the Immigration Service, Department of Labor, without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states that he made a thorough investigation of the case and arrived at the conclusion that Mr. Izard was improperly dismissed from the service. fans hal Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of 
this order

April 23, 1915. 
Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. The above order was issued on request of the Postmaster General, who stated that these men were highly desirable as messengers, entirely trustworthy, and had rendered excellent service, having been directly connected with the office of the Postmaster General since the beginning of the present administration.

Mr. Bernard R. Jett may be transferred in the Office of the Secretary of the Interior from wireman on the per diem roll to electrician at $1,000 per annum. He has been employed intermittently since Sep- ember 9, 1902, has passed the examination for electrician, and by reason of extensive and varied electrical work has become familiar with the complicated systems of light- ing, being one of the few persons who will be able to assist materially in the prepara- tion of long deferred electrical plans for the several buildings. The action proposed will also save several hundred dollars annually by permitting the continuous employ- ment of skilled mechanics who must otherwise be laid off when their services can not well be spared.

of matron and nurse. The Apache prisoners having been removed to the Mescalero Agency, N. Mex., it is desired to appoint Miss Deery as nurse in the Indian Service. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation for this order. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Enna Wilson Noel may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the War Department without regard to the requirements of the civil service rules. Mrs. Noel is the widow of Edward McC. Noel, whose death on April 16, 1915, termi￾nated a service of nearly 33 years in the office of the Surgeon General, and leaves her dependent upon employment for support. Prior to her marriage she served as clerk in the office of the Surgeon General from December 18, 1893, to February 9, 1900, and previously in other offices since November 7, 1889. Her reinstatement is recom- mended by the Secretary of War and the Surgeon General of the Army. The Civil ServicesCommission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 11, 1915. 
Mrs. Laura F. Richmond may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Treasury in view of the efficient service rendered by the husband of Mrs. Richmond in the Treasury Department for 28 years, and in view of the fact that Mr. Richmond is now wholly incapacitated both mentally and physically for the performance of duty, and also because of the satisfactory service rendered by Mrs. Richmond while a former employee in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing where she served for a period of 
seven years. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 13, 1915. 
Michael L. Eidsness, jr., of Iowa, a minor clerk of class D ($900) in the Post Office Department, may be promoted to the position of clerk without further civil service examination. This order was issued upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General, who stated that while Mr. Eidsness was not able to pass the first-grade examination he had a very exceptional record in the Post Office Department and was engaged on clerical work of high order; accomplished without apparent effort 50 per cent more work than any of the clerks with whom he was associated. Mr. Eidsness made three attempts to pass the first-grade examination, but on account of lack of early education was unable to pass. 
May 14, 1915. 
Mr. James J. Harley may be reinstated to a position in the post office at Philadel- phia, Pa. without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Harley was a clerk in the Philadelphia post office from June 1, 1893, to November 15,1900, when heresigned. Hisrecord during that time was entirely satisfactory. His reinstatement is recommended by the postmaster at Philadelphia, who states that he is personally acquainted with Mr. Harley and feels that he is mentally and physically 
capable of performing with satisfaction and efficiency the duties of a postal clerk. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
May 14, 1915. 
Mr. Bernard R. Jett may be transferred in the Office of the Secretary of the Interior from wireman on the per diem roll to electrician at $1,000 per annum. Mr. Jett is employed on the ‘‘ Repair of Buildings” roll in a position for many years not regarded by the department as classified. He was one of a small number whose retention and reemployment without a competitive status were authorized by an executive order of June 17, 1909. He has been employed intermittently since Sep- ember 9, 1902, has passed the examination for electrician, and by reason of extensive and varied electrical work has become familiar with the complicated systems of light- ing, being one of the few persons who will be able to assist materially in the prepara- tion of long deferred electrical plans for the several buildings. The action proposed will also save several hundred dollars annually by permitting the continuous employ- ment of skilled mechanics who must otherwise be laid off when their services can not well be spared.

In view of these facts the commission concurs with the department in recommending the transfer of Mr. Jett by executive order. 
May 14, 1915. 
Mr. Carroll W. Dunning may be reinstated in the Office of Markets and Rural Organization in the Department of Agriculture, where his services are needed to cooperate with the Forest Service in investigations in the marketing of woodlot Products He served as statistician in forest products from November 1, 1911, to arch 16, 1914, and the department states that he has had unusually valuable training and experience at home and abroad. Since leaving the service he has been engaged in a marketing proposition, representing on the Pacific coast a number of eastern manufacturers, this employment being in line with his qualifications and experience. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Agriculture with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
May 25, 1915. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Mr. Albert J. Phillips as associate chemist at $2,000 per annum in the service of the Bureau of Standards, Department of Commerce, at Pittsburgh, Pa. Mr. Phillips was in the service from August 13, 1906, to June 15, 1913, when he resigned. He is especially recommended by the Director of the Bureau of Standards on account of his satisfactory and efficient service. Difficulty has been experienced in obtaining a suitably qualified person for filling the position. : The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this Executive order because of Mr. Phillips long and efficient service, the comparatively short period of his separation from the service, and the need of an employee with his training, which it has been difficult to meet through the usual procedure. 3 
May 27, 1915. 
Mrs. Burr J. Ramage may be appointed a clerk in the classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with civil service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, in view of the faithful and meritorious services of her deceased husband in the Government service, and also in view of the fact that Mrs. Ramage is without means of support, 
June 1, 1915. 
Mrs. F. Pierard may be appointed as seamstress or flagmaker at the navy yard, Mare Island, Cal., without reference to the civil service rules or navy yard regulations. Mis. Pierard’s husband was

128 THIRTY-SECOND REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, 
August 16, 1915. 
Miss Edna M. Ricketts, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the classified service of the Government without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Ricketts is the daughter of the late Thomas T. Ricketts, a veteran of Company C, Thirty-ninth Ohio Volunteer Infantry, who was an employee in the Government Printing Office from July, 1900, until the time of his death in April, 1913. She is an experienced stenographer and typewriter, and is the sole support of her widowed mother (now 74 years of age). : The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case. 
August 19, 1915. 
First Sergeant William Feldman, United States Army, retired, may be admitted to 
examination for the classified service. Paragraph 1, civil-service Rule V, which provides that no person shall be admitted to examination unless he be a citizen of or owe allegiance to the United States, is hereby waived in his favor. Mr. Feldman is technically not a citizen of the United States, notwithstanding his service in the Army. In view of his honorable Army service of over 25 years, he being retired as first sergeant of Troop F, Sixth Cavalry, the commission concurs with the Secretary of War in recommending that Mr. Feldman be admitted to examination under waiver of the rule and with the understanding that he will without delay take the necessary steps to acquire citizenship. 
August 25, 1915. 
Mr. Robert W. F. Ogilve, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the Naturalization Division of the Department of Labor without reference to the requirements of the civil-service rules. The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of this order. 
August 25, 1915. 
Mr. C. Virgil Hinkle may be appointed to a competitive classified position in the postal service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Hinkle was employed as a clerk in the Conway, Ark., post office from July 1, 1898, to June 28, 1913, when he was removed for insubordination, mistreatment of registered mail, and failure to comply with request of post-office inspectors to make good losses of registered mail for which, from circumstantial evidence, it was believed he wasresponsible. The assistant postmaster in office at the time of the embezzlement has confessed to rifling the mail in question. The Conway post office became classified on December 1, 1910, but Mr. Hinkle was not given a competitive classified status. 
This order is recommended by the Postmaster General, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
August 26, 1915. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Green A. Stephens in the postal service. 
Mr. Stephens was a carrier in the San Francisco post office from June 23, 1891, to April 12, 1905, when he was removed upon the charge of tampering with mail addressed 
to a patron in his district and using a race-track admission ticket contained in a letter so addressed. A careful reinvestigation by a post-office inspector resulted in the con￾clusion that beyond any reasonable doubt Mr. Stephens was not guilty of the charge for which he was removed from the postal service. The Postmaster General states that there is no question in his mind but that a distinct injustice was done in separating Carrier Stephens from the service on the flimsy and prejudiced evidence which was adduced in the case. He therefore recommends that an Executive order be issued to reinstate him in the service, and the Civil Service Commission, after careful review of the case, concurs in this recommendation. 
September 2, 1915. 
Miss Bertha Goldberg, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce, without 
reference to the civil-service rules. . Miss Goldberg has passed the stenographer and typewriter examination with an average of 84.29, and has been serving temporarily in the bureau since February 25, 1915. The chief of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce and the Acting Secretary of Commerce recommend her permanent appointment on account of her unusual ability and efficiency as a stenographer and typewriter and the exceptional

The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
September 8, 1915. 
Mr. Clifford B. Potter may be reinstated in the postal service without reference to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Potter was appointed a substitute carrier in the Jersey City, N. J., post office on September 15, 1896, through examination. On January 11, 1900, he was made a regular carrier at $600 and was promoted four times, reaching $1,200, the highest grade, onJuly 1,1908. Heresigned on March 31,1912. The Postmaster General recommends the issuance of this order, as it appears that Mr. Potter's resignation was tendered because his application for leave on account of illness was refused, which request, in the judgment of the Postmaster General’s office, should have been granted. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Potter. 
September 14, 1915. 
James O. Brockenshire, chief musician, United States Army, retired, may be appointed as inspector of musical instruments at $780 per annum, Quartermaster Corps of the Army, without examination under the civil-service rules. The Acting Secretary of War states that the waiving of the civil-service rules to authorize the appointment of Mr. Brockenshire is requested by the Acting Quarter- master General of the Army, in view of his long service in the Army as chief musician and his varied experience with Army bands, which especially qualify him for the position. The Acting Quartermaster General reports that he is a thorough musician, able to play almost any instrument in Army bands, and is just the type of inspector needed by the depot quartermaster at Philadelphia, under whom he has been em- ployed at different times during the past two years, rendering entirely satisfactory service. .Mr. Brockenshire was in the military service as musician for nearly thirty years, voluntarily retiring on June 1, 1914, with a “most excellent character.” During his service, with the exception of about one year, he was with the Seventh Cavalry.
